goldens.comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/serializers/user_serializer.rb:43 — website_name` bypasses the `restrict_user_fields?` gate on `website`, leaking a hidden TL0 website host and path to anonymous API consumers.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, `website_name` is added as a new attribute in the serializer (line 43) and has its own `include_website_name` method that only checks `website.present?`. However, the existing `website` attribute likely has access controls via `restrict_user_fields?` (referenced in the finding as a gate for TL0 users). The new `website_name` attribute doesn't appear to have the same restriction - it's added to the main attributes list without any trust level gating. This means `website_name` could expose website information (host and path) even when `website` itself would be restricted. The `include_website_name` method only checks if website is present, not whether the user should have access to see it.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/serializers/user_serializer.rb:144 — Dropping the first label treats unrelated tenants such as `foo.github.io` and `bar.github.io` as one domain and exposes the full attacker-controlled path.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a security issue in the website_name method at line 144. The code compares domains by dropping the first label (website_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.') == discourse_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.')). For domains like foo.github.io and bar.github.io, this would compare 'github.io' == 'github.io' and return true, treating them as the same domain. This would cause the full path to be exposed (website_host + URI(website.to_s).path) for unrelated tenants on shared hosting platforms, which is a security concern as it could expose attacker-controlled paths.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/serializers/user_serializer.rb:149 — The one-way suffix check fails for a website on a child host of the instance, so `blog.example.com` on `example.com` silently loses its path.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real edge case bug. Looking at the website_name method in user_serializer.rb (lines 137-150), the logic handles three cases: (1) exact match, (2) same-level subdomains (www.example.com vs forum.example.com), and (3) instance being a subdomain of website (example.com vs forum.example.com via ends_with?). However, there's no case for when the website is a subdomain of the instance domain (blog.example.com website on example.com instance). In this case, none of the conditions match: website_host != discourse_host, the subdomain length check fails or the comparison fails, and discourse_host.ends_with?('.blog.example.com') is false. So it falls through to just returning website_host without the path, losing the path information.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/serializers/user_serializer.rb:141 — Case-sensitive host comparison rejects DNS-equivalent URLs such as `https://EXAMPLE.COM/user`, silently omitting their path.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the host comparison in website_name method uses case-sensitive string comparison (e.g., `website_host == discourse_host` on line 141). In Ruby, string comparison with `==` is case-sensitive, so 'EXAMPLE.COM' != 'example.com'. While URI parsing typically normalizes the host to lowercase, the code doesn't explicitly ensure this, and the comparison could fail for URLs with uppercase hostnames. This would cause the path to be omitted when it should be included. The test cases only use lowercase URLs, so this edge case isn't covered.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/serializers/user_serializer.rb:43 — website_name` bypasses the existing untrusted-user field filter and exposes a hidden website host/path to anonymous callers.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that `website_name` is added to the serializer attributes list (line 43) but is NOT added to the `untrusted_attributes` list that controls visibility for untrusted users. Looking at the existing code pattern, `website` is in `untrusted_attributes` (visible in the serializer structure), but the new `website_name` field is only added to the regular attributes. This means `website_name` could be exposed to anonymous/untrusted callers even when `website` itself would be hidden, creating an information disclosure vulnerability.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/serializers/user_serializer.rb:153 — The filter hook lacks the required `?`, so responses for users without websites still gain a `website_name: null` field instead of preserving the optional response shape.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims the filter hook lacks a required '?' but the diff clearly shows at line 155-156 that there is an 'include_website_name' method that returns 'website.present?'. This is the standard Rails serializer pattern where 'include_<attribute>' methods control whether an attribute is included. The method properly checks if website is present, so website_name will only be included when there's a website. The finding misreads how Rails serializers work.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/serializers/user_serializer.rb:153 — The unrecognized `include_website_name` hook (missing `?`) leaves `website_name` serialized for anonymous TL0 profiles and exposes the website that `untrusted_attributes` deliberately hides.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue. Looking at the diff, `include_website_name` is defined without a `?` suffix (line 155-157), but Rails serializers use the convention `include_<attribute>?` to determine whether to include an attribute. Without the `?`, this method won't be recognized as the inclusion guard. Additionally, `website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes` (visible in the serializer structure), which means it should be hidden for anonymous/low-trust users. Since `website_name` doesn't have a working inclusion guard and isn't in `untrusted_attributes`, it could expose website information that should be hidden. This is a security/correctness bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/serializers/user_serializer.rb:144 — Stripping the first label treats unrelated tenants under multi-label public suffixes such as `foo.github.io` and `bar.github.io` as the same domain and incorrectly reveals the full path.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real bug in the website_name method. Looking at lines 141-144, when comparing domains like 'www.example.com' vs 'forum.example.com', the code strips the first label and compares the rest. This logic would incorrectly treat 'foo.github.io' and 'bar.github.io' as the same domain (both become 'github.io' after stripping), causing the full path to be revealed for unrelated tenants on public suffixes. The condition `website_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.') == discourse_host.split('.')[1..-1].join('.')` doesn't account for public suffix lists.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/serializers/user_serializer.rb:149 — The suffix check is directional, so a website on a child host of the instance (for example `blog.example.com` for `example.com`) is incorrectly treated as a different domain and loses its path.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a bug in the website_name logic. Looking at line 149 in the diff: `discourse_host.ends_with?("." << website_host)` - this checks if the discourse host ends with the website host (e.g., 'forums.example.com'.ends_with?('.example.com')). However, the reverse case is not handled: when the website is on a subdomain of the instance (e.g., website is 'blog.example.com' and instance is 'example.com'), the code falls through to just returning `website_host` without the path. The condition `discourse_host.ends_with?("." << website_host)` would be false in this case ('example.com'.ends_with?('.blog.example.com') is false), so it would return just 'blog.example.com' instead of 'blog.example.com/path'. This is a real logic bug where child domains of the instance lose their paths.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/serializers/user_serializer.rb:141 — Host comparison is case-sensitive even though DNS names are not, so URLs such as `https://EXAMPLE.COM/user` fail to show their path on an `example.com` instance.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the website_name method comparing website_host == discourse_host directly (line 141) and using string operations like ends_with? without normalizing case. Since DNS hostnames are case-insensitive but Ruby string comparison is case-sensitive, a URL like 'https://EXAMPLE.COM/user' would have website_host='EXAMPLE.COM' which would not equal discourse_host='example.com', causing the path to not be shown when it should be. This is a real correctness bug in the new code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/serializers/user_serializer.rb:43 — website_name` bypasses the `restrict_user_fields?` gate applied to `website`, exposing a TL0 user's hidden website host and path to anonymous clients.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, `website` is defined in the serializer with an `include_website?` method that likely checks `restrict_user_fields?` (this is a common pattern in Discourse serializers for untrusted_attributes). The new `website_name` attribute is added to the same attributes list but only has `include_website_name` which checks `website.present?` - it does not check the same restriction gate. This means `website_name` could expose the website host/path even when `website` itself would be hidden due to trust level restrictions. The finding correctly identifies a security issue where the new field bypasses existing access controls.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/serializers/user_serializer_spec.rb:11 — The anonymous TL0 test neither sets a website nor covers website_name, so it misses that the new field exposes a website value when website itself is restricted.

adjudication.rationale: The finding raises a valid concern about test coverage. Looking at the diff, the `website_name` method is added to the serializer and includes `include_website_name` which checks `website.present?`. The existing anonymous TL0 test (referenced at line 11) tests untrusted attributes but doesn't set a website. The concern is that `website_name` could potentially expose website information even when `website` itself might be restricted for anonymous users. However, looking at the serializer code, `website` is in the regular attributes list (not `untrusted_attributes`), and `include_website_name` depends on `website.present?`. The finding points to a legitimate gap in test coverage for the new `website_name` field in the context of anonymous/TL0 users, though it's not clear from the diff alone whether this is actually a security bug or just missing test coverage.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/serializers/user_serializer_spec.rb:82 — The same-domain tests use only lowercase hosts, missing that hostname comparison is case-sensitive and an uppercase-equivalent website host loses its path.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue. Looking at the `website_name` method in the serializer, it compares `website_host == discourse_host` directly without case normalization. URI parsing typically preserves case, and while hostnames are case-insensitive per RFC, Ruby string comparison is case-sensitive. If a user enters 'http://Example.com/user' and the discourse host is 'example.com', the comparison would fail and only return 'Example.com' without the path. The tests only use lowercase hosts ('example.com', 'discourse.org', 'forums.example.com'), so they don't catch this edge case. This is a legitimate bug where case-insensitive hostname matching should be used.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/serializers/user_serializer_spec.rb:87 — No test exercises the new equal-depth sibling-subdomain branch such as www.example.com versus forums.example.com, leaving that behavioral case unverified.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a missing test case. Looking at the diff, the `website_name` method in user_serializer.rb has a branch for when `website_host.split('.').length == discourse_host.split('.').length` and both have more than 2 parts (the sibling subdomain case like www.example.com vs forum.example.com). The tests added only cover: (1) different domains entirely, (2) same domain, and (3) parent domain case (forums.example.com with example.com website). There is no test for the equal-depth sibling subdomain branch (e.g., www.example.com website with forums.example.com instance), which is a distinct code path in the implementation.
